clue.text: Curiously a ruling's unique

indicators.note: curiously means in an odd, strange fashion, telling us to arrange the letters of the fodder oddly

parts.note: the 's is kept here as an S, so the word gives all seven letters r-u-l-i-n-g-s

explanation.surface: A judge's decision is described as one of a kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curiously' is the anagram signal: shuffle A plus RULINGS (the S of the possessive counts as a letter).
explanation.definitionFit: Something singular is remarkable and without equal, one of a kind.

clue.text: Keeping feline in, a pen is crazy.

indicators.note: keeping ... in says the pen holds the feline within it, a container signal split around the fodder
completes 'keeping ... in', saying the feline sits inside the pen

parts.note: a sty is a pen for pigs
a cat is a feline

explanation.surface: Someone who shuts a cat in a pig-pen must be mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeping ... in' puts CAT inside STY, the pig-pen.
explanation.definitionFit: Scatty is British informal for scatterbrained or dotty.

clue.text: Inner tum is churning — time for food

indicators.note: a churning stomach has its contents stirred about, so these letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A hungry stomach rumbling signals it is time to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan prints 'tum' (stomach), which OCR read as 'turn'. 'is churning' shuffles INNER TUM into NUTRIMEN, then T for time is added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Nutriment is nourishment, whatever sustains a body as sustenance.

clue.text: Bring a friend in? Can't, being unsociable

indicators.note: bring ... in tells us to place the friend inside another word, a container signal
completes 'bring ... in', putting the friend within the other piece

parts.note: can't means is not capable, unable
a companion is a friend

explanation.surface: Someone asked to bring a friend along has to admit they have nobody to bring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bring ... in' places COMPANION inside UNABLE (from 'Can't'), after its UN.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone uncompanionable shuns company, keeping to themselves.

clue.text: She follows one, not being different

indicators.note: follows says the female pronoun comes after the other pieces in the answer

parts.note: a is the indefinite article, meaning one
her is the object form of she

explanation.surface: A woman queues behind someone, but insists she is not unlike them.
explanation.walkthrough: A (one) and NOT, then HER (she) 'follows' them.
explanation.definitionFit: Another thing is a different one, a further or other alternative.

clue.text: Following operation I consumed a sleep inducing drug

indicators.note: following says the next pieces come after the operation in the answer

parts.note: ate means consumed

explanation.surface: After surgery a patient took a sedative.
explanation.walkthrough: OP, then 'Following' it, I and ATE (consumed).
explanation.definitionFit: An opiate is a narcotic derived from the poppy that dulls pain and brings drowsiness.

clue.text: National prose is peculiar to oneself

indicators.note: peculiar means strange or odd, telling us the letters are rearranged into an odd order

explanation.surface: A country's literary style is unique to the writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peculiar' looks like part of the phrase 'peculiar to oneself' but is the anagram signal: all fifteen letters of NATIONAL PROSE IS are shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Personalisation is making a thing belong or apply to an individual, tailoring it to one's own self.

clue.text: Showing spirit -. having 'a drink about four

indicators.note: about means around, so the drink goes round the number

parts.note: ale is a drink, beer
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Someone lively has a drink around four o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts ALE round IV, the Roman four.
explanation.definitionFit: Being alive in this sense means lively and spirited, full of energy.

clue.text: Church service comprising plainchant

parts.note: even means plain, smooth and level
a song is a chant

explanation.surface: A church service consists of unadorned Gregorian singing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plainchant' is one word on the page, but it splits into PLAIN (EVEN) and CHANT (SONG); 'comprising' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Evensong is the evening prayer service of the Anglican church, also called vespers.

clue.text: Pulley left for one to put aside

indicators.note: left for one says the letter for left replaces the letter for one

parts.note: a sheave is the grooved wheel of a pulley
a is one, the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A mechanic sets aside a pulley he has left over.
explanation.walkthrough: SHEAVE is the grooved wheel of a pulley; 'for' swaps its A (one) for L (left).
explanation.definitionFit: To shelve a plan is to postpone or set it aside.

clue.text: Athenian garret

explanation.surface: A rooftop room in ancient Athens.
explanation.definitionFit: Attic means relating to Athens or its region Attica, and an attic is a room in the roof space, a garret.

clue.text: I sew in a different way

definitions.text: I sew in a different way

parts.words: I sew in a different way
parts.note: the four letters of 'I sew' arranged another way spell a word meaning manner, and 'different' plus that word is also a phrase for differently

explanation.surface: A tailor explains a change of stitching method.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearranged, I SEW gives WISE, an old word for manner (as in 'in no wise'); 'other' plus WISE describes that rearrangement and also means 'in a different way'.
explanation.definitionFit: Otherwise means differently, in another manner.

clue.text: Expressing doubt in test, yet — winning out

indicators.note: in places the doubtful noise inside the test

parts.note: a trial is a test
umph, a variant of humph, is a grunt of doubt

explanation.surface: A doubter of a test result still comes out on top.
explanation.walkthrough: UMPH, a variant spelling of 'humph', goes 'in' TRIAL; 'yet' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Triumphal means celebrating or marking a victory.

clue.text: Literally nothing shuts up

parts.note: the letter O, read literally as a shape, is nought or nothing
pens means shuts up, as sheep in a fold

explanation.surface: Nothing, absolutely nothing, will close.
explanation.walkthrough: O is the figure nought; PENS means shuts up. The whole clue also gives the sense: where nothing shuts, everything is open.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that opens unfastens or unshuts, the reverse of closing up.

clue.text: Commercial song is one way to make sound

parts.note: a rep is a commercial traveller, a sales representative
an air is a song or tune

explanation.surface: An advertising jingle is one way to put things right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commercial' suggests an advert but is the salesperson, REP; 'is one way to' links.
explanation.definitionFit: To repair something is to fix it, making it whole again.

clue.text: Clansman doffed his cap, showing high spirits

indicators.note: to doff a cap is to take off what sits on top, so the word loses its first letter

parts.note: a clansman is a relation, a kinsman

explanation.surface: A Highlander tipped his bonnet, visibly cheerful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doffed his cap' removes the R at the front of RELATION.
explanation.definitionFit: Elation is great happiness and exhilaration.

clue.text: Fat Auntie, unlikely to exercise 'charm'

indicators.note: exercise suggests working the letters out, and unlikely says the result is improbable, so the auntie's letters are shuffled

explanation.surface: A stout aunt, never one for the gym, is still charming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unlikely to exercise' signals the anagram of FAT AUNTIE.
explanation.definitionFit: To infatuate is to inspire a foolish passion in someone, to bewitch them.

clue.text: Discharge task, following easy start

indicators.note: following puts the task after that letter in the answer
start means the first letter of the word easy

parts.note: a mission is a task

explanation.surface: Being let go from a job after an easy beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: E, the start of 'easy', then MISSION 'following' it.
explanation.definitionFit: An emission is something given off or released, as fumes from an exhaust.

clue.text: Becoming tangled, coupling takes time

indicators.note: takes means holds inside, so the coupling surrounds the letter

parts.note: mating is coupling, as animals do

explanation.surface: Getting entangled, a pair of animals take their time.
explanation.walkthrough: MATING 'takes' T inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair or fibres that are matting are clumping into knots, getting snarled.

clue.text: Sandy is plucky…

explanation.surface: A person named Sandy is courageous.
explanation.definitionFit: Gritty means full of grit, like sand, and also brave and determined.

clue.text: Heads of whiting and herring — dubious and smelly

indicators.note: heads means the first letters of each of the two fish

parts.note: iffy is informal for dubious

explanation.surface: Fish of questionable freshness give off a stink.
explanation.walkthrough: W and H, the 'Heads of' whiting and herring, then IFFY.
explanation.definitionFit: Whiffy is British slang for giving off an unpleasant odour.

clue.text: … Walter's dissipated and profligate

indicators.note: dissipated means scattered, so these letters are dispersed into a new order

parts.note: the 's is kept as an S, giving seven letters

explanation.surface: Following on from plucky Sandy, Walter has led a dissolute and wasteful life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dissipated' scatters WALTERS. The dots join it to 19 'Sandy is plucky', making Sandy and Walter a pair; the OCR's stray '21' is not on the page.
explanation.definitionFit: A wastrel is a spendthrift good-for-nothing who squanders money.

clue.text: Brush around yard and closet

indicators.note: around says the brush goes round the abbreviation

parts.note: a broom is a brush

explanation.surface: Sweep round the garden and the cupboard.
explanation.walkthrough: BROOM goes 'around' Y (yard), giving B-Y-ROOM.
explanation.definitionFit: A by-room is a small side room or private chamber, the old sense of closet.

clue.text: In this a London drawing-room

indicators.note: in says the answer is held inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A capital drawing-room is described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' signals the letters running across 'thiS A LONdon'.
explanation.definitionFit: A salon is a reception room in a grand house, a parlour for guests.

clue.text: Thrashed and braided

explanation.surface: Beaten and then plaited.
explanation.definitionFit: To lace someone is to beat or whip them, and laced hair or cord is interwoven or plaited.

clue.text: At this very moment in time; left in a nasty mess

indicators.note: a mess is a jumble, so these letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Right now, someone has been abandoned in an awful muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: IN, then T, L and NASTY jumbled ('mess') to give STANTLY; 'in a' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Instantly means immediately, without any delay.

clue.text: See brooding hen suffer.., covering battery egg

indicators.note: covering means going over and round, so the first word encloses the rest

parts.note: to incur is to suffer, as a loss
O is an egg by its shape

explanation.surface: Look how a battery hen suffers while sitting on her egg.
explanation.walkthrough: INCUR is 'covering' BAT and O. 'See' asks the solver to picture the device as a stand-in hen.
explanation.definitionFit: An incubator keeps eggs warm to hatch them, doing the sitting bird's work.

clue.text: Setter's: past the perfect state

parts.note: the setter refers to themselves as I, and setter's stands for I am
ago means in the past

explanation.surface: The compiler looks back on an ideal former condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter's' is I'M; AGO is past. 'Perfect' suggests grammar's perfect tense, but it is the insect's final adult stage.
explanation.definitionFit: An imago is the fully developed adult form of an insect, its final complete stage.

clue.text: An idiot is oddly tinged

indicators.note: oddly means in a strange way, telling us the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A fool has a curious colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' rearranges TINGED.
explanation.definitionFit: Nidget is an archaic word for a fool or simpleton.

clue.text: Being nimble, he designed this palace

indicators.note: designed means planned and laid out, so these letters are laid out afresh

explanation.surface: An agile architect drew up the plans for a grand house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'designed' rearranges NIMBLE HE. BLENHEIM Palace in Oxfordshire is the Churchill family seat, designed by Vanbrugh.
explanation.definitionFit: Blenheim Palace is a stately home in Oxfordshire, birthplace of Winston Churchill.
